question: Do common sparse-autoencoder reconstruction and LLM-based explanation metrics identify features produced by training, or can comparably high scores arise from random transformer weights, stable token identity, and generic architectural or data structure?

key_findings.claim: Aggregate fuzzing and detection auto-interpretability scores often overlap between trained and randomized Pythia transformers at larger scales, but the title is broader than the actual result: small-model curves distinguish several variants, and the paper itself qualifies the conclusion as holding only in many settings.
key_findings.evidence: The 6.9B fuzzing curves overlap and the 1B/6.9B randomized variants sometimes exceed the trained model, supporting the core warning that a high aggregate AUROC is not sufficient evidence of learned computation. However, the appendix plots show visible trained-versus-re-randomized gaps at 70M and 160M, while Step-0 can differ from both. Only 100 eligible latents per layer/variant are evaluated, and uncertainty across five seeds is shown only for Pythia-70M. The defensible conclusion is therefore metric insufficiency and scale-dependent overlap, not universal inability to distinguish trained and random transformers.

key_findings.claim: The related-work account understates direct prior art: Bricken et al. had already reported that automated interpretability can score randomized-transformer SAE features more highly because of a single-token mode.
key_findings.evidence: Page 3 says Bricken et al.'s auto-interpretability scores 'discriminated effectively' between a random and trained one-layer transformer. The primary 2023 study is more nuanced and more damaging to novelty: its randomized-transformer features had a higher median automated score, driven by a distinct population of trivial single-token features; trained features became preferable after isolating non-single-token features and under manual or downstream-logit analyses. The current paper extends that phenomenon across Pythia scale and null variants and adds entropy, but it is not the first observation that random lexical SAE features can receive high automatic scores.

key_findings.claim: The strongest explanation for high auto-interpretability in the random variants is stable lexical identity, not evidence that the SAE recovered a learned mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: Every non-control variant retains a deterministic token-ID-to-vector map even when the embedding values are random, whereas the negative control resamples a fresh Gaussian embedding for every token occurrence and uniquely destroys stable identity. Across the 80 feature dashboards, re-randomized and Step-0 features are overwhelmingly exact token or subword detectors with near-zero entropy and often very high AUROC; trained late-layer dashboards contain some broader semantic features but also many lexical ones. Thus the control is an intentionally easy lexical-null condition, not a matched random-initialization control, and the classifier mostly tests whether an explanation predicts surface activation patterns.

L Example Feature Dashboards for Pythia-6.9B

key_findings.claim: Reconstruction quality and explanation predictability are not functional faithfulness: only the trained model has meaningful language-model loss recovery, even when randomized models reconstruct well and score highly on auto-interpretability.
key_findings.evidence: Cosine reconstruction, explained variance, sparsity norms, and auto-interpretability can be similar across trained and random variants. In contrast, the cross-entropy loss-recovered score is meaningful only for the trained model because every randomized transformer already has very poor language loss with either original or SAE-reconstructed activations. The experiment therefore supplies a negative result about proxy validity but no functional comparison showing that random features mediate useful behavior.

key_findings.claim: Token-distribution entropy separates the three regimes better than aggregate AUROC, but it is an exploratory lexical-specificity proxy rather than a validated measure of abstraction.
key_findings.evidence: Randomized features generally combine low entropy with high AUROC, the per-occurrence Gaussian control has high entropy and near-chance AUROC, and trained later-layer features include a high-entropy/high-AUROC region. Yet entropy is computed from activation-weighted top examples above an implementation threshold, normalized by vocabulary size, and is sensitive to BPE segmentation, token frequency, feature selection, dataset coverage, and activation scale. Figure 20 supplies no regression coefficients, uncertainty, matched-frequency controls, human abstraction labels, counterfactual paraphrases, or causal intervention tests.

key_findings.claim: The apparent closing of the trained-randomized gap with model scale is confounded by simultaneous growth in the underlying transformer, residual width, SAE dictionary width, and feature specificity.
key_findings.evidence: The default expansion factor is fixed at 64, so increasing Pythia width also increases the number of SAE latents. The authors themselves speculate that larger dictionaries produce more specific features that are easier for the LLM classifier to describe. Cross-size plots therefore cannot isolate transformer scale from dictionary capacity, token-feature granularity, activation distribution, or explainer behavior. The hyperparameter sweeps cover only selected 160M and 1B configurations and do not hold dictionary width fixed across model sizes.

key_findings.claim: The published artifact contradicts the stated all-parameter re-randomization: the experiment configuration preserves trained LayerNorm parameters in both re-randomized variants by default.
key_findings.evidence: The paper says all parameters, including embeddings in one variant, are resampled from per-matrix Gaussians. In the official ICLR supplemental code, ExperimentConfig sets rerandomize_layer_norm=False, the run scripts never enable the corresponding flag, and train/evaluation/activation scripts pass that value to the re-randomizer, which skips parameters whose names match LayerNorm patterns. The two headline re-randomized nulls therefore retain learned normalization parameters in addition to any explicitly retained embeddings, while the true Step-0 null follows a different parameter-scale distribution.

key_findings.claim: The toy experiments make preservation or amplification of sparse structure plausible, but they do not establish that random transformers create superposition or explain the language-model result.
key_findings.evidence: A linear map preserves a sparse latent generative form, although the displayed Gaussian notation incorrectly places z where the transformed observation should appear. For the nonlinear toy, a random two-layer ReLU network narrows the SAE Pareto gap between structured inputs and a globally moment-matched Gaussian control, but ReLU mechanically creates exact zeros and nonnegativity. Figure 3 calls a pseudoinverse of a non-square 2-by-3 projection an inverse and plots a coordinate projection of the MLP output rather than a native MLP layer. The Gaussian control matches only global scalar moments, per-example normalization is undisclosed in the paper, plotted seed uncertainty is absent, and no toy feature ground truth exists after the MLP.

anchors.section: 4.1 Matrix Multiplications Preserve Superposition and Figure 3

key_findings.claim: The official supplemental artifact is not a runnable or provenance-complete reproduction of the reported study.
key_findings.evidence: The 1.29MB ICLR supplemental ZIP contains 188 original files and 26,893 Python lines, but no git commit, checkpoints, result tables, raw auto-interpretability records, or complete pinned main environment. It is visibly stale relative to the 2026 paper revision, retains the earlier ICML title, and vendors partial copies of three projects. Static execution checks find a duplicate-keyword SyntaxError, a malformed 160M shell script, missing imported project modules, and no tests. Most run scripts use --dont_train and fixed defaults, so the released bundle cannot regenerate the trained SAEs or final plots from a clean environment. This matters because several critical choices are absent or inconsistent in prose, including feature eligibility/selection, 410M layer stride, LayerNorm preservation, and pooling of AUROC examples.

key_findings.claim: The evaluation sample is less transparent and less directly random than the prose suggests, and aggregate AUROC hides feature-level heterogeneity.
key_findings.evidence: The paper states that 100 features are randomly sampled for each SAE. The released pipeline first samples a larger candidate pool, rejects features without at least 200 activation occurrences, sorts eligible IDs within buffers, and stops after the first 100 encountered; this is not a documented uniform sample over all live features. Plotting code micro-pools classifier labels and predictions across features within a layer rather than averaging per-feature AUROC, supplies no confidence interval outside the 70M seed plot, and places the final plotted layer's AUC values in the Figure 1 legend. Consequently, a high aggregate can be dominated by easy lexical features and does not imply that a typical or tail feature is well explained.

method.core_idea: Apply a model-parameter randomization sanity check to SAE evaluation: train comparable per-layer SAEs on trained, re-randomized, true-initialization, and token-identity-destroying transformer variants, then ask which metrics actually respond to learning.
method.mechanism: For Pythia 70M through 6.9B, collect residual-stream activations from five model variants, train TopK SAEs on RedPajama tokens, and compute reconstruction, sparsity, loss-recovery, LLM-generated explanation, fuzzing, detection, and token-entropy metrics. The re-randomized variants sample each weight matrix from a Gaussian using that trained matrix's mean and variance, either retaining or replacing embeddings; Step-0 uses the original initialization checkpoint; the negative control replaces every token occurrence with fresh standard-Gaussian input. Separate linear, Sharkey-style sparse-data, GloVe, and embedding toys test whether random maps can preserve or increase SAE-recoverable sparse structure.
assumptions: Aggregate LLM-classifier AUROC is a useful proxy for whether a latent has a faithful natural-language explanation, even though it measures activation predictability rather than causal role.

A transformer with re-randomized weights is an appropriate null for learned computation despite preserving architecture, deterministic token identity, trained per-matrix moments, and, in the released code, trained LayerNorm parameters.
The per-occurrence Gaussian embedding control is informative even though it removes stable token identity and is therefore much harder than every other variant.
One hundred selected eligible features represent each SAE's feature distribution and micro-pooled AUROC represents feature-level quality.
Results across model sizes reflect scale rather than the simultaneous increase in SAE dictionary width and token-feature specificity.
The Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct quantized explainer/scorer behaves comparably across trained, random, lexical, and nonsensical feature regimes.
Activation-weighted token entropy over selected top examples tracks abstraction despite vocabulary, frequency, BPE, threshold, and sample-selection effects.
A random ReLU MLP's improved reconstruction-sparsity frontier is evidence about superposition rather than primarily the point mass at zero induced by ReLU and preprocessing.
Per-matrix Gaussian moment matching preserves enough scale structure to make trained and re-randomized comparisons meaningful, while Step-0 provides a useful separately scaled initialization control.
The qualitative conclusions from Pythia and RedPajama generalize enough to motivate broad SAE-evaluation practice, although the paper explicitly limits its empirical claim to this family and dataset.

techniques.role: Compares trained Pythia checkpoints with per-matrix Gaussian re-randomization and true Step-0 checkpoints.
Destroys deterministic token identity by resampling every input embedding occurrence from a standard Gaussian.
Learns default expansion-64, k=32 sparse reconstructions of each sampled residual-stream layer.
Tests whether an LLM can identify correctly marked activating and non-activating token examples given a generated feature explanation.
Tests whether an LLM can identify which examples contain activating tokens for a feature.
Measures how concentrated activation mass is over token IDs among high-activation examples.
Measures the functional language-loss effect of substituting SAE reconstructions relative to zero ablation.
Repeats the Pythia-70M metric calculation with five random seeds to estimate limited uncertainty.
Retrains selected SAEs with 1M, 100M, or 1B tokens to test undertraining and data-scale robustness.
Varies expansion and TopK sparsity on selected Pythia sizes.
Uses known sparse generative features and SAE recovery to calibrate a reconstruction-sparsity proxy.
Passes structured, embedding, and Gaussian inputs through a random two-layer ReLU MLP and compares SAE Pareto frontiers.
Displays two sampled feature dashboards per layer and variant for qualitative inspection of lexical versus semantic behavior.

evaluations.setting: Per-layer TopK SAEs trained on 100M RedPajama tokens from trained, two re-randomized, Step-0, and Gaussian-embedding-control Pythia models from 70M to 6.9B parameters.
evaluations.metric: Fuzzing and detection AUROC from 100 selected features per SAE using Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4.
evaluations.result: Random and trained curves substantially overlap at 410M, 1B, and 6.9B and random variants can score higher at large scale; visible gaps remain at 70M and 160M, while the occurrence-wise embedding control stays near chance.
evaluations.baseline: The fully trained checkpoint, true Pythia Step-0 checkpoint, and the deliberately identity-destroying Gaussian input control.

evaluations.setting: The same Pythia/model-variant matrix and SAE reconstructions.
evaluations.metric: Cosine similarity, explained variance, reconstruction error, L1/L2 activation norms, and related standard SAE proxies.
evaluations.result: Most random variants are closer to the trained model than to the Gaussian embedding control; Step-0 often differs because its parameter scales differ from the trained-moment re-randomization.
evaluations.baseline: Metrics for trained-model SAEs and the per-occurrence Gaussian embedding control.

evaluations.setting: SAE substitution into the forward pass of each underlying Pythia variant.
evaluations.metric: Cross-entropy loss recovered relative to zero ablation.
evaluations.result: The metric is informative for the trained transformer but not for randomized variants, whose base language loss is already poor regardless of original versus reconstructed activations.
evaluations.baseline: Original activations and zero-ablated activations within each model variant.

evaluations.setting: Selected Pythia-6.9B features across model layers and all five variants.
evaluations.metric: Activation-weighted token-ID entropy and its per-latent relationship to fuzzing AUROC.
evaluations.result: Randomized variants cluster at low entropy with a negative entropy-AUROC relationship; the control has high entropy and low AUROC; trained later layers contain some high-entropy, high-AUROC features. No statistical or human abstraction validation is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Trained, three randomized/initialization variants, and the occurrence-wise Gaussian control.

evaluations.setting: Pythia-70M and 410M SAEs retrained on 1B rather than 100M tokens, plus Pythia-1B SAEs trained on 1M versus 1B tokens.
evaluations.metric: The same reconstruction, sparsity, loss-recovery, AUROC, and token-entropy panels.
evaluations.result: Increasing to 1B tokens preserves the qualitative comparisons. At 1M tokens, explained variance and loss recovery degrade strongly and AUROC falls in later layers, showing that auto-interpretability is not wholly insensitive to SAE undertraining.
evaluations.baseline: The 100M-token main runs and the 1B-token Pythia-1B runs.

evaluations.setting: Pythia-70M evaluation repeated across five random seeds.
evaluations.metric: Uncertainty bars for the full metric panel.
evaluations.result: The five-seed plot provides the only explicit multi-seed uncertainty analysis; corresponding uncertainty is not shown for the larger models that support the headline overlap claim.

evaluations.setting: Pythia-160M expansion factors 16 through 128 with k in {16,32}, and Pythia-1B including an extreme expansion-2, k=4 setting.
evaluations.metric: Standard SAE metrics, auto-interpretability, and token entropy.
evaluations.result: Moderate hyperparameter changes preserve relative trends; the tiny Pythia-1B SAE is clearly worse on reconstruction and loss recovery while retaining surprisingly similar auto-interpretability.

evaluations.setting: Ten thousand Sharkey-style samples generated from 512 sparse features in 256 dimensions, with standard L1 SAEs and ten nominal toy seeds.
evaluations.metric: Mean maximum cosine similarity to the known feature dictionary and explained-variance/sparsity Pareto frontiers before and after a random two-layer ReLU MLP.
evaluations.result: SAEs recover the input dictionary in a Goldilocks regularization range; structured inputs dominate globally moment-matched Gaussian inputs, but the Pareto gap shrinks after the random ReLU MLP.
evaluations.baseline: Globally mean/standard-deviation-matched Gaussian input and output controls.

evaluations.setting: GloVe 50/100/200/300-dimensional vectors and Pythia embedding matrices passed through random two-layer ReLU MLPs.
evaluations.metric: Explained-variance versus normalized L1 sparsity Pareto frontiers.
evaluations.result: Embedding inputs show smaller structured-versus-Gaussian gaps than the synthetic sparse data, and both input types become easier for an L1 SAE after ReLU. The paper says GloVe uses one seed, while the supplemental shell/config defaults specify ten.
evaluations.baseline: Global-scalar-moment-matched Gaussian vectors before and after the same MLP.

evaluations.setting: Eighty Pythia-6.9B feature dashboards, two sampled features per shown layer and model variant.
evaluations.metric: Top activating token windows, explanation text, token entropy, and fuzzing AUROC.
evaluations.result: Randomized and Step-0 examples are dominated by exact token/subword identity features with high AUROC; trained later layers include some more semantic or phrase-level cases, while the control examples are diffuse and frequently nonsensical. These are illustrative rather than a blinded human evaluation.
evaluations.baseline: Side-by-side trained, randomized, Step-0, and occurrence-wise Gaussian-control dashboards.

limitations: Author-stated: the study covers only Pythia models and RedPajama-V2 activations, so it does not establish the same behavior for other model families, modalities, or data distributions.
Author-stated: it uses one default open-source explainer/scorer configuration; different LLMs and explanation pipelines may change absolute or relative scores.
Author-stated: the result does not show that trained-model SAEs contain no additional learned information; it only shows that aggregate metrics are insufficient evidence for that information.

Reviewer inference: the negative control uniquely destroys stable token identity on every occurrence and is therefore much easier to distinguish than a random transformer with deterministic embeddings.
Reviewer inference: trained-model size, residual dimension, SAE dictionary size, and feature specificity co-vary, confounding the scale interpretation.
Reviewer inference: only 70M receives a five-seed uncertainty analysis; headline larger-scale plots have no error bars or disclosed model/SAE randomization sweep.

Reviewer inference: the selected 100 features are filtered by activation occurrence and are not sampled by the simple uniform procedure described in prose; micro-pooled AUROC can hide feature-level tails.

Reviewer inference: the trained-moment re-randomization preserves layerwise scale information and the released code also preserves trained LayerNorm parameters, so it is not an all-parameter random null.

Reviewer inference: token entropy is a BPE- and corpus-dependent lexical-specificity statistic, not a direct metric of conceptual abstraction, compositionality, causal relevance, or out-of-distribution faithfulness.

Reviewer inference: no matched functional metric compares trained and random variants because randomized language models lack useful cross-entropy behavior; no intervention, steering, causal mediation, circuit, or downstream task is used for the central comparison.

Reviewer inference: the toy Gaussian controls match only global scalar moments, while ReLU itself creates zeros and the non-square pseudoinverse visualization can make arm-like coordinates appear without demonstrating latent superposition.

Artifact audit: the official supplemental bundle is stale, incomplete, and non-runnable as released; missing modules, a SyntaxError, a malformed shell script, absent checkpoints/results, and no git revision prevent clean reproduction.

Specification audit: the paper does not disclose the 200-occurrence feature eligibility rule, selection-order behavior, AUROC micro-pooling, 410M main/control layer-stride mismatch, or preservation of LayerNorm parameters.

Visual audit: most cross-layer figures lack uncertainty, Figure 1's legend values come from the final displayed layer rather than an across-layer aggregate, and dashboard examples are not a blinded or statistically representative semantic study.
failure_modes: An explanation metric can reward exact token detectors because a concise lexical rule predicts held-out examples even when the underlying model has learned nothing about the concept.
A null that destroys token identity can make every deterministic-embedding model appear meaningfully structured, exaggerating evidence for learned representations.
Micro-averaging across features can let common easy examples dominate while rare, polysemantic, or badly explained features disappear from the aggregate.
Increasing SAE width can split features into narrower lexical detectors, raising automatic scores without increasing causal or conceptual fidelity.
Moment-matched randomization can retain trained scale profiles or normalization parameters, leaking training-dependent structure into the null.
An explainer and scorer from the same LLM family can share lexical priors and agree with each other while both are wrong about a feature's causal role.
Top-activation-only explanations can have high precision and poor recall, failing on paraphrases, semantic near-negatives, adversarial triggers, and low-activation contexts.
Token entropy can label multi-token lexical mixtures as abstract and fragment one semantic concept across BPE tokens, reversing rankings under a different tokenizer or corpus.
ReLU-induced zeros and preprocessing normalization can make random-network outputs easier for an SAE even if no meaningful sparse latent causes generated them.
A feature can reconstruct activation variance yet be functionally irrelevant, or preserve loss while using a decomposition unrelated to the model's actual computation.
Single-seed scaling plots can mistake one random initialization, one SAE sample, or one eligible-feature sample for a systematic scale law.
A stale or incomplete artifact can silently implement a different null or feature sampler from the paper, making apparent replications incomparable.
reusable_insights: Randomization tests should preserve nuisance structure while selectively breaking the claimed causal source; use a ladder of nulls for weights, embeddings, normalization, token identity, data order, and trained scale rather than one extreme control.
Report both macro-per-feature and micro-per-example explanation metrics, full score distributions, eligibility rates, dead-feature rates, and stratification by token entropy and activation frequency.

Separate lexical description from mechanistic explanation by testing paraphrases, same-token different-context examples, semantic near-negatives, counterfactual substitutions, and downstream interventions.
Hold SAE dictionary width and sparsity fixed when studying model scale, then separately sweep expansion ratio to identify whether score gains come from feature splitting.
Use function-bearing benchmarks or synthetic mechanisms with known ground truth when asking whether a representation reflects learned computation.
Treat loss recovery, reconstruction, explanation predictability, concept coverage, causal control, stability, and abstraction as distinct axes; a single composite score conceals important tradeoffs.
Audit null implementations directly: LayerNorms, embeddings, tied weights, biases, optimizer state, and per-layer scale can survive nominal randomization.
Validate automatic explanation metrics against blinded human judgments and falsification sets before using them to compare architectures or claim scaling progress.
For token-specific features, compare against direct token-ID baselines; an SAE should have to add explanatory power beyond vocabulary identity.
Publish the exact sampled feature IDs, activation records, prompts, classifier outputs, aggregation code, seeds, checkpoints, and environment so aggregate curves can be decomposed and reproduced.
open_questions: What matched null preserves token identity, activation covariance, LayerNorms, and scale while selectively removing information learned from next-token prediction?
Do trained-model features outperform randomized features on causal mediation, steering specificity, counterfactual invariance, and downstream behavior after matching token frequency and entropy?
Can explanation evaluation be decomposed into lexical identity, local context, semantic class, relation, algorithmic state, and causal consequence, with a separate calibrated score for each level?
How much of the apparent scale trend remains when transformer width, SAE dictionary width, sparsity, activation frequency, and explainer capacity are independently controlled?
Would macro-averaged AUROC, precision-recall, calibration, and worst-decile performance reverse the rankings produced by micro-pooled AUROC?
How stable are the paper's entropy and AUROC conclusions across tokenizers, corpora, sampling thresholds, feature seeds, random transformer seeds, and explanation models?
Can a supervised abstraction dataset or human protocol validate token entropy against genuinely relational, compositional, and context-invariant features?
Which trained information is actually present in SAE latents above a deterministic token-ID baseline, and where across layers does that incremental information appear?
Does fully re-randomizing LayerNorms reproduce the published curves, and how do per-matrix trained-moment, initialization-distribution, entry-shuffle, and spectral-preserving nulls differ?
Can toy studies distinguish ReLU's mechanical zeros from recovery of an identifiable sparse latent model after the random nonlinear map?
How do feature explanations behave on close negatives, paraphrases, feature-trigger tokens inserted into unrelated text, and semantically positive examples without the usual trigger tokens?
Can a clean, pinned reproduction recover the reported figures from released checkpoints and records, or do the artifact's hidden choices materially change the conclusions?

competitive_landscape.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
competitive_landscape.difference: Adebayo et al. establish that an explanation method should respond to model parameters and data by progressively randomizing vision networks. The present paper transfers that logic to SAE training and auto-interpretability, but its nulls additionally change activation distributions and token identity in ways that require matched controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. test GPT-4 neuron explanations observationally and interventionally, finding high error and little causal efficacy even for confident explanations. It predates this paper's random-model test and directly supplies the causal validation axis missing from fuzzing/detection AUROC.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Cunningham et al. report greater automated interpretability than neuron baselines and localize causally responsible IOI features. Heap et al. challenge the sufficiency of the automated score, while Cunningham et al.'s task-specific causal analysis represents stronger evidence than aggregate explanation AUROC alone.

competitive_landscape.title: RAVEL: Evaluating Interpretability Methods on Disentangling Language Model Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: RAVEL defines controlled attribute-value tasks and causal interchange criteria, finding a distributed subspace method stronger than neuron-level approaches. It operationalizes learned functional disentanglement rather than asking whether an LLM can describe top activations.

competitive_landscape.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Braun et al. train dictionaries through downstream KL rather than activation reconstruction alone, explicitly targeting network function. This addresses Heap et al.'s finding that reconstructable random activations can look interpretable without mediating useful language behavior.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Gao et al. introduce k-sparse SAEs, scaling laws, and multiple feature-quality metrics, and report that explanation-related metrics improve with dictionary size. Heap et al. use this architecture but show that dictionary growth can also make random lexical features score well, confounding interpretability scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring Progress in Dictionary Learning for Language Model Interpretability with Board Game Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Karvonen et al. use chess and Othello ground-truth board properties and find trained transformers materially better than random-weight controls. Their supervised concepts distinguish model knowledge in a domain where Heap et al.'s language auto-interpretability curves often overlap, showing that the conclusion depends strongly on metric and data regime.

competitive_landscape.title: Algorithmic Capabilities of Random Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhong and Andreas show fixed random transformer interiors can support nontrivial algorithms when embeddings are trained. Heap et al. freeze or randomize embeddings and study representational proxies, so high SAE scores do not imply those capabilities, but the work cautions against equating random weights with absence of all useful architectural computation.

competitive_landscape.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Paulo et al. introduce the open fuzzing/detection pipeline used here and also propose intervention scoring and warn about scoring pitfalls. Heap et al. stress-test its aggregate observational classifiers on random nulls but do not run the intervention scorer that better targets downstream effects.

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Targeted Concept Erasure Tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Karvonen et al. automate spurious-cue removal and targeted probe perturbation to measure concept disentanglement. These tasks can distinguish architectures and hyperparameters using functional consequences, complementing the null sensitivity that aggregate explanation AUROC lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features
competitive_landscape.difference: Paulo and Belrose find major feature-set variation across SAE seeds, especially for TopK SAEs, arguing for pragmatic rather than canonical dictionaries. Heap et al. expose a different non-identifiability: high explanation scores can persist when the underlying transformer is randomized.

competitive_landscape.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: AxBench compares SAEs with prompting, finetuning, difference-in-means, probes, and representation finetuning, finding SAEs noncompetitive on steering and concept detection in its original evaluation. It supplies direct task baselines absent from the random-null study and demonstrates that interpretability proxies need not predict utility.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: Leask et al. use SAE stitching and meta-SAEs to show incompleteness and non-atomicity across dictionary sizes. Their result explains why larger dictionaries and high interpretability scores need not converge to a unique feature ontology, reinforcing Heap et al.'s scale confound.

competitive_landscape.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: SAEBench aggregates reconstruction, auto-interpretability, disentanglement, probing, unlearning, and control tasks and finds proxy gains do not reliably transfer to practical performance. It directly operationalizes the multi-axis evaluation response called for by Heap et al., although no single benchmark metric is definitive.

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating SAE Interpretability Without Explanations
competitive_landscape.difference: Paulo and Belrose remove natural-language explanation generation as an intermediate variable and compare direct feature-quality measures with human judgments. This targets the confounding between explainer quality and latent quality exposed by random lexical features.

competitive_landscape.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Tian et al. generate semantically similar texts and find many apparently interpretable features fail to activate, with sensitivity declining as SAE width grows. This directly tests the high-precision/low-recall failure that top-example fuzzing and token entropy can miss.

competitive_landscape.title: Revising and Falsifying Sparse Autoencoder Feature Explanations
competitive_landscape.difference: Ma et al. use semantically close negative sentences, structured multi-component explanations, and iterative revision, finding ordinary explanation methods overly broad and recall-biased. Their falsification sets are substantially harder than the random negatives and stable-token classifications used here.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Ye et al. find feed-forward key/value vectors nearly match SAEs on modern interpretability benchmarks and sometimes outperform them. The result reinforces the need for baselines beyond random controls before attributing high scores to the learned SAE decomposition itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
competitive_landscape.difference: Ma et al. show putative reasoning features often fire from a few associated tokens, and LLM-guided counterexamples falsify the remainder; steering produces little benefit. This directly confirms Heap et al.'s concern that lexical correlates can masquerade as abstract features and supplies stronger counterfactual tests.

competitive_landscape.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
competitive_landscape.difference: Korznikov et al. randomize SAE directions or activation patterns and find random-constrained baselines nearly match trained SAEs on interpretability, probing, and causal editing, while synthetic SAEs recover little ground truth despite high explained variance. It broadens the sanity check from random underlying transformers to random SAE decompositions and adds functional metrics.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
competitive_landscape.difference: Makelov et al. use a supervised IOI feature dictionary and separately test approximation, interpretability, and intervention control, finding unsupervised SAEs less successful at controlling the computation. This provides a function-grounded reference that random-model activation-description scores cannot replace.

competitive_landscape.title: Tokenized SAEs: Disentangling SAE Reconstructions
competitive_landscape.difference: Dooms and Wilhelm show that many residual-stream SAE features encode simple token/input statistics and introduce a per-token bias that separates token reconstruction from residual structure. This directly explains why stable random token embeddings can yield high lexical AUROC without a learned transformer computation.

competitive_landscape.title: Enhancing Automated Interpretability with Output-Centric Feature Descriptions
competitive_landscape.difference: Gur-Arieh et al. show that input/top-activation descriptions can miss a feature's causal output effect and propose output-centric descriptions evaluated with steering. This directly targets the functional meaning omitted by fuzzing and detection of input activation patterns.

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating Neuron Explanations: A Unified Framework with Sanity Checks
competitive_landscape.difference: Oikarinen et al. introduce missing- and extra-label sanity checks and find that ROC AUC fails the extra-label test while several alternative metrics pass both. The result directly pressures this paper's reliance on fuzzing/detection AUROC, although the exact Delphi prompts and sampling scheme still require a dedicated replication.

competitive_landscape.title: Descriptive Collision in Sparse Autoencoder Auto-Interpretability: When One Explanation Describes Many Features
competitive_landscape.difference: McCann shows that detection-style scoring can remain high when one generic description fits many distinct features and proposes collision-adjusted discrimination. This is a structural failure beyond the random lexical mode: activation predictiveness does not establish that an explanation uniquely identifies a feature.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Sparse Autoencoder Benchmarks Reliable?
competitive_landscape.difference: Chanin audits SAE benchmarks with reseed noise, synthetic-ground-truth correlation, and training-trajectory discrimination, finding canonical metrics noisier or less discriminative than assumed and several downstream tasks failing multiple lenses. It extends the null-test principle from models and features to the benchmark metrics themselves.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Encode Both Concepts and Functions: The Downstream Geometry of Feature Effects
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoang et al. find that clear activation descriptions often coexist with weak, context-dependent, or multidirectional downstream effects and that stable one-dimensional causal effects are rare. This sharpens the central distinction between lexical interpretability and functional interpretation that the random-transformer study identifies but does not measure.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that common aggregate SAE reconstruction and auto-interpretability metrics frequently fail a trained-versus-random-transformer sanity check across Pythia scales, and proposes token-distribution entropy as an initial measure of feature abstractness.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Its empirical contribution is the five-variant, multi-scale Pythia comparison, the joint metric panels, training-data and hyperparameter checks, 80 feature dashboards, and toy exploration of sparse structure through random maps. It also makes the important distinction between explanation predictability and learned computational relevance.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The novelty is narrower than a first discovery that random-transformer SAE features can score highly: Bricken et al. had already reported automated scores favoring single-token features in a randomized one-layer transformer, and Karvonen et al. had compared trained and random board-game models with ground-truth features. Heap et al.'s defensible advance is scale, multiple null variants, a systematic metric comparison, and an explicit lexical-entropy diagnosis. The strongest conclusion survives the audit—aggregate observational SAE metrics are insufficient—but the all-parameter null is contradicted by preserved LayerNorms, the control is unmatched, larger-scale uncertainty is missing, and the artifact cannot reproduce the study cleanly. Subsequent falsification and random-baseline work substantially strengthens and broadens the paper's warning.

reviewer_notes: Read all 81 pages of arXiv v2 (submitted 2025-01-29, revised 2026-01-27; published at ICLR 2026), including every appendix, reference, equation, metric definition, toy specification, and dashboard. Visually inspected all 66 visual-bearing pages at original 120dpi renders: five main-result/toy pages, appendix metric panels on pages 15-34, the compute table on page 41, and all 80 two-feature dashboard pages on pages 42-81. Audited the complete arXiv source package: 114 files excluding the downloaded tarball, including 107 PDF and four PNG visual assets plus TeX/bibliography/style/manifest files. No standalone official repository was discoverable by exact-title, arXiv, author, or public-repository search as of 2026-08-23, but the official ICLR proceedings supplemental ZIP was found and audited (SHA-256 b6320aa50020bc8e9b84980406a0a1758d398551258ff7ef7ba8616539d588e3): 230 archive entries, 188 original files, 150 Python files, and 26,893 Python lines. Compile, shell-syntax, import, dependency, provenance, sampling, plotting, configuration, and toy-code audits found the material artifact issues reported above; no experiment was rerun because the delivered pipeline lacks required modules, checkpoints, result records, and a runnable environment. Twenty-seven primary arXiv/OpenReview/PMLR/NeurIPS competitors were checked through 2026-08-23. Material contradictions are the broad title versus scale-qualified evidence; the incomplete characterization of Bricken et al.'s direct random/single-token prior; stable token identity versus the unmatched per-occurrence Gaussian control; paper-stated all-parameter randomization versus code-preserved trained LayerNorms; simple random feature sampling versus filtered/order-dependent selection; cross-size scale claims versus dictionary-width confounding; entropy-as-abstraction language versus an unvalidated lexical proxy; and the nonlinear toy interpretation versus ReLU/pseudoinverse/control confounds. The central empirical warning remains credible and is supported by later work, but it should be stated as insufficiency of aggregate proxies rather than equivalence of trained and random representations.
